title: Dates and Times
summary: Do math with dates, pull out their parts, and format them.
intro: Due dates, birthdays, and monthly reports all need date math. PostgreSQL can add days and months, measure gaps, pull out parts, and format dates however you like.

steps.title: Date math
steps.body:
This lesson uses two tables. `rentals` tracks movie rentals in 2025, and `returned_on` is NULL for a movie that is still out. `members` holds birthdays.

```sql
CREATE TABLE rentals (id integer, title text, rented_on date, due_on date, returned_on date);
-- (1, 'The Matrix', '2025-01-03', '2025-01-10', '2025-01-09'), ...
-- (7, 'Coco', '2025-12-22', '2025-12-29', NULL)
CREATE TABLE members (id integer, name text, born date);
-- (1, 'Ana', '1990-07-01'), (2, 'Ben', '1985-12-15'), ...
```

A date plus or minus an integer moves by that many days, and one date minus another gives the days between them as an integer:

```sql
SELECT DATE '2025-03-01' - 1 AS day_before, DATE '2025-03-10' - DATE '2025-03-01' AS days;
-- 2025-02-28 | 9
```

For months, weeks, or years, use an interval such as `INTERVAL '1 month'` or `INTERVAL '2 weeks'`. A date plus an interval gives a timestamp, `2025-04-01 00:00:00`, so cast it back with `::date`. Wrap the sum in parentheses first, because `::` binds tighter than `+`. Months have different lengths, so PostgreSQL clamps to the last day: `DATE '2025-01-31' + INTERVAL '1 month'` is February 28. As always, NULL in gives NULL out.

example.title: Rental timeline
example.prompt: For each rental, show how many days it was kept, a last chance date one week after it was due, and the same day one month after it was rented.
example.code:
SELECT title,
    returned_on - rented_on AS days_kept,
    due_on + 7 AS last_chance,
    (rented_on + INTERVAL '1 month')::date AS next_month
FROM rentals
ORDER BY id;
example.explanation: `returned_on - rented_on` subtracts two dates, so it is a whole number of days, and Coco gets NULL because it has no return date. `due_on + 7` adds days and stays a date. Adding `INTERVAL '1 month'` makes a timestamp, and `::date` turns it back into a date. Look at Spirited Away and Arrival: January 31 and May 31 land on the last day of the shorter next month.

practice.title: Late returns
practice.prompt:
Show how late each rental came back and when a two week rental would end.

1. Select `title` from `rentals`.
2. Add `days_late`: the return date minus the due date. Early returns give a negative number, and a movie still out gives NULL.
3. Add `two_weeks`: the rental date plus `INTERVAL '2 weeks'`, cast to a date.
4. Sort by `id`.

Expected output:

```text
     title     | days_late | two_weeks
---------------+-----------+------------
 The Matrix    |        -1 | 2025-01-17
 Spirited Away |         3 | 2025-02-14
 Inception     |         0 | 2025-02-28
 Up            |         6 | 2025-04-13
 Arrival       |        -2 | 2025-06-14
 Heat          |         7 | 2025-08-29
 Coco          |           | 2026-01-05
(7 rows)
```
practice.starter:
-- TODO: add the days_late and two_weeks columns
SELECT title
FROM rentals
ORDER BY id;
practice.solution:
SELECT title,
    returned_on - due_on AS days_late,
    (rented_on + INTERVAL '2 weeks')::date AS two_weeks
FROM rentals
ORDER BY id;
hints: Subtracting one date from another gives a number of days.
Wrap the sum in parentheses before `::date`. Without them the cast applies to the interval alone, which is an error.

steps.title: Parts of a date
steps.body:
`extract(field FROM date)` pulls one number out of a date. Common fields are `YEAR`, `MONTH`, `DAY`, `DOW` (day of the week, 0 for Sunday), and `QUARTER`.

```sql
SELECT extract(YEAR FROM DATE '2025-03-14') AS y, extract(DOW FROM DATE '2025-03-14') AS dow;
-- 2025 | 5
```

`to_char(date, pattern)` formats a date as text. `YYYY` is the year, `MM` the month number, `DD` the day, `Mon` a short month name, and `Day` the weekday name. Anything else in the pattern, like `/` or `, `, is copied as is.

The gotcha: `Day` pads every name to 9 characters, so `'Friday'` comes out as `'Friday   '`. Put `FM` (fill mode) in front, as `FMDay`, to drop the padding.

`date_trunc('month', date)` rounds a date down to the first day of its month, `'year'` gives January 1, and `'week'` goes back to Monday. It returns a timestamp with a time zone, `2025-03-01 00:00:00+00`, so cast it with `::date`. It is the usual way to put dates into monthly buckets.

example.title: Pretty rental dates
example.prompt: For each rental, show the month number, a friendly date, the weekday, and the first day of the month it was rented in.
example.code:
SELECT title,
    extract(MONTH FROM rented_on) AS month,
    to_char(rented_on, 'Mon DD, YYYY') AS pretty,
    to_char(rented_on, 'FMDay') AS weekday,
    date_trunc('month', rented_on)::date AS month_start
FROM rentals
ORDER BY id;
example.explanation: `extract` returns a plain number, so the month is right-aligned. The pattern `'Mon DD, YYYY'` mixes codes with literal text: `Mon` becomes `Jan`, and the comma and spaces stay. `FMDay` gives the weekday with no trailing spaces. `date_trunc` keeps the year and month, sets the day to 1, and `::date` drops the time.

practice.title: Due date details
practice.prompt:
Show the parts of each rental's due date.

1. Select `title` from `rentals`.
2. Add `month`: the month number of `due_on`.
3. Add `due`: `due_on` formatted as day, month, and year with slashes, like `10/01/2025`.
4. Add `weekday`: the weekday name of `due_on` with no padding.
5. Add `month_start`: the first day of the month of `due_on`, as a date.
6. Sort by `id`.

Expected output:

```text
     title     | month |    due     | weekday  | month_start
---------------+-------+------------+----------+-------------
 The Matrix    |     1 | 10/01/2025 | Friday   | 2025-01-01
 Spirited Away |     2 | 07/02/2025 | Friday   | 2025-02-01
 Inception     |     2 | 21/02/2025 | Friday   | 2025-02-01
 Up            |     4 | 06/04/2025 | Sunday   | 2025-04-01
 Arrival       |     6 | 07/06/2025 | Saturday | 2025-06-01
 Heat          |     8 | 22/08/2025 | Friday   | 2025-08-01
 Coco          |    12 | 29/12/2025 | Monday   | 2025-12-01
(7 rows)
```
practice.starter:
-- TODO: add the month, due, weekday, and month_start columns
SELECT title, due_on
FROM rentals
ORDER BY id;
practice.solution:
SELECT title,
    extract(MONTH FROM due_on) AS month,
    to_char(due_on, 'DD/MM/YYYY') AS due,
    to_char(due_on, 'FMDay') AS weekday,
    date_trunc('month', due_on)::date AS month_start
FROM rentals
ORDER BY id;
hints: Use `MM` for the month number and `DD` for the day.
Inside a `to_char` pattern, `/` is copied as is, so put it between the codes.
Fill mode `FM` in front of `Day` removes the padding.

steps.title: Ages and date ranges
steps.body:
`age(later, earlier)` returns the gap between two dates as an interval in years, months, and days, the way people say ages. Always pass a fixed date as the first argument: `age(born)` alone measures from today, so its answer changes every day.

```sql
SELECT age(DATE '2025-07-01', DATE '1990-03-01');
-- 35 years 4 mons
```

For whole years, take the `YEAR` field of that interval with `extract`. Dividing a day count by 365 drifts because of leap years, so let `age` do the counting. Someone whose birthday is the reference date has just turned a year older, and someone whose birthday is the next day has not.

`generate_series` from the loops lesson also counts over dates when you give it an interval step: `generate_series(DATE '2025-03-01', DATE '2025-03-07', INTERVAL '1 day')`. Each value is a timestamp with a time zone, so cast it with `::date`. Use a step like `INTERVAL '7 days'` or `INTERVAL '1 month'` to skip ahead. The stop date is included only when a step lands exactly on it.

example.title: Member ages and one week
example.prompt: Show each member's age on July 1, 2025 and their whole years, then list the first week of March 2025 with weekday names.
example.code:
SELECT name,
    age(DATE '2025-07-01', born) AS age,
    extract(YEAR FROM age(DATE '2025-07-01', born)) AS years
FROM members
ORDER BY id;

SELECT d::date AS day, to_char(d, 'FMDay') AS weekday
FROM generate_series(DATE '2025-03-01', DATE '2025-03-07', INTERVAL '1 day') AS d
ORDER BY day;
example.output:
name  |           age           | years
-------+-------------------------+-------
 Ana   | 35 years                |    35
 Ben   | 39 years 6 mons 17 days |    39
 Chloe | 24 years 4 mons 1 day   |    24
 Dev   | 46 years 9 mons 1 day   |    46
(4 rows)

    day     |  weekday
------------+-----------
 2025-03-01 | Saturday
 2025-03-02 | Sunday
 2025-03-03 | Monday
 2025-03-04 | Tuesday
 2025-03-05 | Wednesday
 2025-03-06 | Thursday
 2025-03-07 | Friday
(7 rows)
example.explanation: Ana was born on July 1, so on the reference date she is exactly 35 years. Ben is 39 years and some months, and `extract(YEAR ...)` keeps only the 39. In the second query `generate_series` makes one timestamp per day, named `d`. The SELECT casts it to a date and formats the weekday.

practice.title: Year end ages and Mondays
practice.prompt:
Show each member's whole years at the end of 2025, then list every Monday in March 2025.

1. Select `name` from `members`.
2. Add `years`: the whole years from `born` to `DATE '2025-12-31'`.
3. Sort by `id`.
4. In a second query, list the Mondays as dates in a column named `monday`. March 3, 2025 is the first Monday, so start there and step 7 days until March 31.
5. Sort the Mondays by `monday`.

Expected output:

```text
 name  | years
-------+-------
 Ana   |    35
 Ben   |    40
 Chloe |    24
 Dev   |    47
(4 rows)

   monday
------------
 2025-03-03
 2025-03-10
 2025-03-17
 2025-03-24
 2025-03-31
(5 rows)
```

DELETE FROM members WHERE id <= 2;
INSERT INTO members (id, name, born) VALUES (7, 'Gus', '2024-12-31');

hints: Put an `age` call with the fixed date first inside `extract(YEAR FROM ...)`.
Give `generate_series` an `INTERVAL '7 days'` step, name it in FROM, and cast each value with `::date`.

recap:
- `date + 7` and `date - 7` move by days, and `date - date` gives the days between.
- `INTERVAL '1 month'` adds months or weeks. Cast the timestamp back with `::date`.
- Adding a month to the 31st clamps to the last day of a shorter month.
- `extract(MONTH FROM d)` pulls out one field as a number.
- `to_char(d, 'Mon DD, YYYY')` formats a date, and `FMDay` drops the padding.
- `date_trunc('month', d)::date` gives the first day of the month.
- `extract(YEAR FROM age(later, earlier))` gives whole years. Always give `age` a fixed later date.
- `generate_series` with an interval step lists dates. Cast each one with `::date`.
